alt: A table showing how functionalists, Marxists and feminists read the same school practices: socialisation and social control, the curriculum, setting by ability, and testing and meritocracy.
caption: The same practice means different things to each view, which is why they are easy to set against each other.

after: ## The Marxist view: education reproduces class inequality
alt: Six Marxist points around reproduction of class inequality: Althusser’s ideological state apparatus, Bourdieu’s cultural capital, the myth of meritocracy from Bowles and Gintis, material factors such as access to devices, setting by ability, and Willis’s lads, who reproduced their class through their own resistance.
caption: Each Marxist concept is a mechanism that keeps working-class children in working-class jobs.

after: ## The feminist view: education perpetuates gender inequality
alt: Six feminist mechanisms: male power in school hierarchies, few female role models in science or leadership, girls’ access to education, a gendered curriculum (Kelly), teacher expectations (Stanworth and Spender) and peer control (Lees). A note says girls now outperform boys in many countries.
caption: Feminists show how gender inequality is built into school life, but must explain girls’ success.

after: ## The feminist view: education perpetuates gender inequality
alt: A table of strengths and limitations of functionalist, Marxist and feminist views of education, including Tumin’s criticism of Davis and Moore, Willis’s evidence of resistance and girls now outperforming boys.
caption: Use each view’s limitations as the starting point for the next view.

alt: A six-step discuss plan: set out the Marxist view, give three distinct mechanisms (correspondence principle, cultural capital, material factors and setting), evaluate with Willis, functionalists and feminists, and end with a judgement that the view overstates passivity.
caption: Three distinct mechanisms, two criticisms, one judgement.
